_about: Horizontal domain-correlation signals: the evidence that ties another registered (apex) domain to a target organization, so an enumeration's scope can be made more complete. docs/ai/HORIZONTALS.md and `amass review horizontal-signals` are generated from this file; edit the rationale here. Each signal's weight times 100 is the confidence the related-domains lens records for a domain the signal supports; a domain found by several signals keeps the strongest. A WHOIS privacy proxy or placeholder organization, and a certificate or name server shared by more apex domains than the lens's cap (provider/CDN infrastructure), are excluded, not scored. A name match alone is never sufficient. The scored runtime scope-expansion decision and the classifier read the same catalog, so the lens, the engine and the model share one source of truth.

signals.title: Shared registrant organization
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose WHOIS/RDAP registrant contact names the same organization as the target's.
signals.rationale: The registrant organization on a domain record is the party that registered the domain, recorded by the registry. When two domains name the same organization as registrant, the same party registered both, which is direct evidence they belong to the same footprint.
guards: A WHOIS privacy or registrar proxy (for example Domains By Proxy, LLC) is never an anchor: thousands of unrelated domains share one, so the match is suppressed (internal/registrant).
A placeholder or redaction organization value is excluded the same way.
A matching organization name alone, with no shared registrant record, is never sufficient: unrelated companies share names across jurisdictions.
counter_indications: Resellers, registrars and agencies sometimes register domains for clients under their own organization.
A parent holding company can be the registrant of record for legally separate subsidiaries.

signals.title: Shared certificate subject organization
signals.finds: The apex domains covered by a TLS certificate (its common name and DNS subject-alternative names) whose subject contact names the organization.
signals.rationale: An organization-validated certificate carries a subject organization the certificate authority verified against the requesting entity. The apex domains such a certificate covers were presented together by that organization, so they tie to its footprint.
guards: A certificate covering more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is treated as shared or CDN infrastructure (many tenants on one certificate), not shared ownership, and is skipped.
A privacy-proxy or placeholder subject organization is excluded.
counter_indications: A hosting or SaaS provider can name itself as the subject organization on certificates it issues for customer domains.
A domain-validated certificate carries no verified organization and does not produce this signal.

signals.title: Shared name server
signals.finds: Another registered domain served by the same authoritative name server as one of the organization's own domains.
signals.rationale: A private or vanity name server operated by one organization serves only that organization's domains, so sharing it is evidence of common control. It is supporting rather than strong because a small hosting provider's shared name server can serve unrelated customers.
guards: A name server inside the organization's own domains gives the strong name-server-own-domain signal instead.
A name server serving more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is treated as shared or provider infrastructure and is skipped.
Only name servers reached from the organization's own domain records are used as anchors.
counter_indications: Managed DNS and small hosting providers run name servers shared by many unrelated customers.
A registrar's default name servers are shared across its whole customer base.

signals.title: Same DNS provider delegation set
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose registration lists exactly the same full set of at least four name servers as one of the organization's own domains, all from a provider that gives each account or hosted zone its own set drawn from a large pool (dns.json assignment unique_set, such as an Amazon Route 53 delegation set).
signals.rationale: Route 53 gives each hosted zone four name servers chosen from thousands, and an account can reuse one delegation set across its zones. An identical full set recurring by chance is vanishingly rare, so two domains sharing it are almost certainly in one provider account. It is supporting rather than strong for scope expansion because one account shows a common operator, not a common owner: agencies, resellers and managed-service providers run many clients' zones from one account. On its own it sends the domain to review; with a strong signal it expands scope. (In ownership gaps, where nothing is collected, the same evidence is the strong dns_provider_unique_set signal.)
guards: The whole set must match: every name server, at least four, all from the one unique_set provider.
Only name servers reached from the organization's own domain records are used as anchors.
A set listed by more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is skipped.
counter_indications: A reseller, agency or managed-service provider can host many clients' zones in its own account, so the domains share an operator rather than an owner.

signals.title: Allowed cross-origin by the organization's site
signals.finds: Another registered domain that a web service on one of the organization's own hosts names in its CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin or CSP frame-ancestors header, letting that domain call or embed it.
signals.rationale: Sites usually let their own sister sites (an application portal, a student system, a regional site) call their APIs or frame their pages, and they name them one by one. It is supporting rather than strong because partners and vendors are allowed the same way.
guards: Only services on the organization's own hosts are read.
Only named origins count: a wildcard (*) or 'null' names no domain.
Never expands scope on its own.
counter_indications: A partner, payment provider or embedding vendor is allowed exactly like a sister site.
Some frameworks echo back whatever origin asked, so the header names the prober's origin rather than a chosen one; Amass's probes send no Origin header.

signals.title: Listed by the organization's bug-bounty program
signals.finds: Another registered domain that a public bug-bounty program lists in scope beside one of the organization's names, when the program is tied to the organization by its website, its exact name, the platform's verification TXT record on the organization's domain, or a link from the organization's security.txt.
signals.rationale: A program's scope is the organization's own public list of the assets it is responsible for, so the other domains it lists are usually the organization's. It is supporting rather than strong because it is review-only evidence: a scope can list a partner's or a vendor's domain, or a subsidiary that is a separate organization.
guards: Only programs tied to the organization count.
Names under cloud providers' hosting domains and the platforms' own sites are skipped.
Never expands scope on its own.
counter_indications: A vendor-hosted tenant or a partner's system can be listed so researchers may test it.
A parent's program can cover subsidiaries and acquisitions that are separate organizations.

signals.title: Shared DIRECT ad seller account
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose ads.txt or app-ads.txt lists, as DIRECT, the same advertising seller account (an ad system and account ID, such as a Google AdSense publisher ID) as one of the organization's own domains.
signals.rationale: A DIRECT line names an ad account the publisher controls itself and is paid through, so it is as specific to its owner as an analytics property: the domains that list it are run by the same publisher.
guards: Only DIRECT lines count; RESELLER lines name the companies that sell on the publisher's behalf.
An account the ad system's sellers.json lists as an INTERMEDIARY (a sales house) is skipped.
An account listed by more than 25 registered domains is treated as a network's, not an owner's, and skipped.
counter_indications: A sales house or agency can list its own account as DIRECT on the sites it manages.
A copied ads.txt can keep a former owner's accounts.

signals.title: Domain an ad system gives for the organization's seller account
signals.finds: The domain an ad system's sellers.json gives as the business domain of the seller behind one of the organization's DIRECT ad accounts, when it is another domain.
signals.rationale: sellers.json names the business behind each account, by name and domain, as the ad system knows it from paying it. A different domain there is usually the publisher's corporate site. It is supporting because the seller can be a parent, an agency or a sales house that the ad system lists as a publisher.
guards: Accounts the ad system lists as INTERMEDIARY or keeps confidential are skipped.
The ad system's own domain is skipped.
Never expands scope on its own.
counter_indications: An agency that manages a site's ads can be the seller of record.
A parent company's domain can be listed for its brands' accounts.

signals.title: Publisher site of the organization's verified Maven group
signals.finds: Another registered domain a package in the organization's Maven Central group names as its publisher's organization URL, where the group is the reverse of one of the organization's own domains.
signals.rationale: Maven Central lets a publisher use a groupId only after proving, with a DNS TXT record, that it controls the domain the groupId names. A package in that group names its publisher's organization in its POM, so the site it names there is the organization's own declaration of its site.
guards: Only groups named for one of the organization's own domains count.
Only the POM's organization URL counts; its project and repository URLs are the supporting package-website signal.
URLs on registries, documentation and code hosts, and cloud providers' hosting domains are never stored.
counter_indications: A POM copied from a parent project or a template can keep another organization's URL.
A group handed to a spun-off project can keep naming the former parent.

signals.title: Named by the organization's published packages
signals.finds: Another registered domain one of the organization's packages names as its homepage, project page or repository: a package in a Maven group named for one of the organization's domains, or an npm package maintained from an address at one.
signals.rationale: A package's homepage and project pages are usually its publisher's sites. It is supporting because a package can point to a community site, a hosted documentation service or a partner's product page.
guards: Only namespaces tied to one of the organization's domains count: a Maven group named for it, or an npm namespace with a maintainer address at it.
URLs on registries, documentation and code hosts, and cloud providers' hosting domains are never stored.
Never expands scope on its own.
counter_indications: An open-source project can live on its own community domain that no organization owns.
A maintainer can keep a work address on a personal project.

signals.title: SOA administrator mailbox at the organization's domain
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose SOA record names, as its zone administrator (RNAME), a mailbox at one of the organization's own domains that one of the organization's zones also names.
signals.rationale: A zone's SOA record names the mailbox of the person responsible for it. A zone whose administrator is a mailbox at the organization's own domain, the same one its own zones list, is run by the organization's DNS staff.
guards: The mailbox must be at one of the organization's own registered domains or a name below one.
A DNS host's default mailbox is skipped: a managed-DNS provider's, or one at the registered domain of a primary name server outside the organization.
A mailbox that more than 25 domains list is skipped.
counter_indications: A zone copied from the organization's template can keep its mailbox after the domain changes hands.
An agency running DNS for a client may list the client's mailbox in zones of its own.

signals.title: Shared SOA administrator mailbox
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose SOA record names the same zone administrator mailbox (RNAME) as one of the organization's zones, when that mailbox is outside the organization's domains.
signals.rationale: The same administrator mailbox in two zones points to one administrator. It is supporting rather than strong for an outside mailbox: a web agency, registrar or IT contractor administers many clients' zones from its own mailbox.
guards: A DNS host's default mailbox is skipped.
A mailbox that more than 25 domains list is skipped.
Never expands scope on its own.
counter_indications: An agency or contractor administers unrelated clients' zones from one mailbox.

signals.title: Name server run by the organization
signals.finds: Another registered domain served by a name server that is a host inside one of the organization's own domains (ns1.example.com serving example-labs.org), the same server one of the organization's domains uses.
signals.rationale: An organization that runs its own name servers hosts its own zones on them. A domain delegated to a name server inside the organization's namespace is served by the organization's DNS, which it rarely does for anyone else.
guards: The name server must be one of the organization's own registered domains or a name below one.
A name server more than 25 domains use is skipped.
A managed-DNS provider's name server is never used.
counter_indications: A university or ISP running DNS for affiliated or customer organizations serves their zones from its own servers.
A delegation can outlive a domain's sale until the new owner moves it.

signals.title: Mail exchanger run by the organization
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose mail is handled by a mail exchanger that is a host inside one of the organization's own domains, the same one one of the organization's domains uses.
signals.rationale: A domain whose mail goes to the organization's own mail server receives its mail at the organization, which an organization does for its own domains and rarely for others.
guards: The mail exchanger must be one of the organization's own registered domains or a name below one.
A mail exchanger more than 25 domains use is skipped.
A known mail provider's exchanger is never used.
counter_indications: An organization can relay mail for affiliated organizations or customers through its own servers.

signals.title: Sends all its mail through the organization
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose SPF record authorizes only names inside the organization's own domains to send its mail, when at most 5 domains authorize the organization's domain.
signals.rationale: A domain that sends all of its mail through the organization, and through no one else, is the organization's: an outside sender would list its own servers or its other providers too.
guards: Every name and address range the domain's SPF record authorizes must be inside the organization's domains.
At most 5 domains may authorize the organization's domain; an email or IT provider is authorized by many.
A known mail-policy provider's domain is never used.
counter_indications: When the organization is itself an email, hosting or IT provider, a small client can send only through it.

signals.title: Shared mail exchanger
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose mail is handled by the same mail exchanger (MX host) as one of the organization's own domains.
signals.rationale: A mail exchanger an organization runs for its own mail serves only that organization's domains, so two apex domains pointing their MX at the same host are evidence of common control. It is supporting rather than strong because a mail provider's exchanger is shared by many unrelated customers; in OAM an MX record is the same shape as a name-server record (an apex FQDN pointing to a server FQDN), so this mirrors the shared-name-server signal.
guards: A mail exchanger inside the organization's own domains gives the strong mx-own-domain signal instead.
A mail exchanger serving more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is treated as a shared mail provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Proofpoint and the like) and is skipped, not scored.
Only mail exchangers reached from the organization's own domains are used as anchors.
counter_indications: Managed mail providers and SaaS email gateways are the MX for many unrelated customers.
A parent company can run one mail system for legally separate subsidiaries.

signals.title: DMARC reports to the organization
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose DMARC record sends its aggregate or forensic reports (rua/ruf) to a domain the organization owns.
signals.rationale: A domain's DMARC record names where its mail-authentication reports are sent. Pointing them at a domain the organization controls is a deliberate administrative act: that organization's mail team collects and acts on the reports, so the two domains are administered together. The reporting address is derived from the published DMARC TXT record, which is kept as evidence.
guards: A reporting domain referenced by more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is a shared DMARC processor (dmarcian, Valimail and the like), not common ownership, and is skipped, not scored.
A reporting domain a known mail-policy provider operates is skipped regardless of how many referencing domains are in the database.
Only the organization's own domains are used as the reporting anchor.
counter_indications: A managed DMARC service receives many unrelated customers' reports at its own domain.
An external reporting destination requires the destination to authorize it, which this signal does not yet verify.

signals.title: SPF authorizes the organization's senders
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose SPF record delegates its sending (include: or redirect=) to a domain the organization owns.
signals.rationale: An SPF include or redirect names a domain allowed to send mail as the publishing domain. Delegating to a domain the organization controls means the organization's mail infrastructure sends on the other domain's behalf, which is evidence of common administration. It is supporting rather than strong because a provider's SPF macro is included by many unrelated customers.
guards: A domain that sends all its mail through the organization, when few domains do, gives the strong spf-authorizes-exclusive signal instead.
An SPF domain referenced by more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is a shared sending provider (a mail provider's SPF macro) and is skipped, not scored.
An SPF domain a known mail-policy provider operates is skipped regardless of coverage.
Only the organization's own domains are used as the SPF anchor.
counter_indications: A hosting or email provider's SPF macro domain is included by all of its customers.
A domain can keep an include for a service it no longer uses.

signals.title: Official website
signals.finds: A domain the organization publishes as its own website (Organization --website--> URL --domain--> FQDN), for example recorded by the Wikidata official-website collector.
signals.rationale: An official website recorded for an organization is a curated, third-party-asserted claim that the organization owns that domain, so it is the strongest of the current horizontal signals.
guards: Only a website edge on the subject organization itself is used.
The apex (registered domain) of the website host is taken, not the full host name.
counter_indications: A curated source can record a campaign or microsite domain hosted by a third party as an official website.
An out-of-date record can name a domain the organization no longer controls.

signals.title: Shared analytics identifier
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose web service embeds the same analytics or tag-manager identifier (a Google Analytics or Tag Manager property, a Facebook pixel and the like) as one of the organization's own services.
signals.rationale: An analytics or tag-manager property is registered to one account and embedded by that account's own sites to report their traffic together. Two sites carrying the same property identifier are administered by the same account, which is strong evidence of common control. The identifier is a shared Identifier asset, so the match is a one-hop graph pivot, not a value scan.
guards: A default or signal-free identifier value is skipped (internal/semantics/fingerprint_defaults.json).
An identifier embedded on more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is treated as a shared marketing or agency account, not common ownership, and is skipped.
Only identifiers on the organization's own services are used as anchors.
counter_indications: A marketing agency can embed one analytics property across several unrelated clients.
A template or theme can ship a placeholder property identifier that several unrelated sites keep.

signals.title: Shared favicon
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose web service serves a favicon with the same hash as one of the organization's own services.
signals.rationale: Organizations reuse one brand favicon across their sites, so two services serving a byte-identical favicon are often the same operator's. It is supporting rather than strong because content-management frameworks and hosting panels ship default favicons that many unrelated sites keep unchanged.
guards: A default or framework favicon hash is skipped (fingerprint_defaults.json).
A favicon served by more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is treated as a shared default or CDN asset and is skipped.
Only favicons on the organization's own services are used as anchors.
counter_indications: A framework, CMS theme or hosting panel ships a default favicon that unrelated sites keep.
A hosting provider can serve one favicon across many parked or placeholder sites.

signals.title: Shared page content
signals.finds: Another registered domain whose web service returns a page body with the same hash as one of the organization's own services.
signals.rationale: A byte-identical, non-trivial page body served from two domains is usually one deployment answering on both, which is evidence of common control. It is supporting because parked, placeholder and default-install pages are identical across many unrelated domains.
guards: A default, parked or placeholder page hash is skipped (fingerprint_defaults.json), and only normalized bodies above a minimum size are hashed at collection.
A body served by more distinct apex domains than the lens cap is treated as a shared parked or default page and is skipped.
Only page bodies on the organization's own services are used as anchors.
counter_indications: Parking services, registrars and hosting providers serve one placeholder body across many unrelated domains.
A CDN error or maintenance page can be identical across unrelated sites.
